reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
Measured adoption of AI in educational services sits at 30.0% in the latest reading from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks whether a business used AI in the last two weeks. The prior period stood at 35.5%, so the most recent figure is lower than the one before it. The Census Bureau notes that the survey first asked this question in September 2023 and that an S marks suppressed values. The figure covers Educational services under NAICS 61.

The federal government's own posture is documented by the Department of Education, which has assembled an inventory of AI use-cases and describes its work as adhering to federal regulations on AI advancement while ensuring responsible and secure usage. The Department's listed uses are largely administrative and instructional support: CAISY for real-time insights, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation; Grammarly's AI assistant for written communication; Otter.AI for real-time transcription and collaboration in meetings, interviews, and lectures; and AWS Bedrock for building applications on foundation models. Other listed uses include generating summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, producing code snippets from written prompts, extracting key points and action items from public documents, generating mock datasets for testing, and training employees on prompt engineering. The Department also describes using fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information to test filters and data loss prevention.

On the market side, HolonIQ is described as a platform for impact market intelligence covering the global impact economy, with capabilities for sizing addressable markets, quantifying demand, forecasting scenarios at varying rates of growth, and mapping competitive landscapes and partnerships. Its page states that it serves governments, institutions, technology companies, global firms, and investors, and that the global media relies on it for insight and data. The excerpt does not report specific funding totals, growth rates, or adoption numbers for education AI.

This site's own cataloguing work covers courses and credentials. The courses page states that 13 AI courses are tracked, 11 of them free, with 3 carrying public companion code, each with a verified source and re-verified daily. It reports that all ten courses tracked there offer free access to core materials, though three pair that with a paid certificate option or public code repositories. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, specifically Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry sources including DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. The page notes that university courses are generally structured around exam-driven theory while the industry courses are described as code-first or hands-on, and that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

The sourced points add that the Department of Education's guidance frames permissible use, risk, and procurement for US education, and that the education sections of this site track the courses and credentials the field actually uses, with costs and renewal cycles pointing at issuer pages. HolonIQ is characterized as the market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed, and workforce learning.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few limited conclusions. The Census Bureau's measure shows roughly a third of educational services firms reporting recent AI use, and the direction between the two periods reported is downward. The Department of Education's inventory shows that a federal education agency itself deploys AI for transcription, drafting, summarization, code generation, and testing of data loss prevention, which indicates these uses are considered acceptable in an education context when paired with responsible and secure usage requirements. The course cataloguing shows that free and low-cost training exists across both university and industry providers, though the sources do not report whether that training changes deployment outcomes. The excerpts do not contain ROI figures, vendor spending totals, or enforcement actions, so nothing can be said about those from this material.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
